title: IT Threat Intel - IT Cybersecurity
description: Curated IT / enterprise cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_threatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Attackers are now exploiting the critical NetScaler authentication bypass — CVE-2026-19490 turns a Gateway or AAA virtual server into unauthenticated access, and roughly 22,000 appliances are still reachable from the internet
items.content_text: Citrix patched CVE-2026-19490 in mid-August and published its advisory on 19 August 2026. The flaw lets an unauthenticated remote attacker bypass authentication when a NetScaler appliance is configured as an AAA virtual server or as a Gateway — SSL VPN, ICA Proxy, CVPN or RDP Proxy — with the exact exposure depending on firmware version and whether a SAML Action is configured. For three weeks that remained a patching problem. It stopped being one on 3 September, when vulnerability-intelligence firm Previdian reported that its NetScaler sensors had picked up exploitation attempts from three distinct IP addresses in Australia, the United States and Germany. A credible proof of concept had been published online shortly before, which is the usual sequence: advisory, PoC, opportunistic scanning, then targeted use. Shadowserver tracks more than 22,000 internet-exposed NetScaler ADC appliances and close to 1,700 Gateway instances, though that count includes patched systems and honeypots and is not a vulnerable-population figure. The reason this sits at the top of the page rather than in the advisory list is what a NetScaler Gateway is: the front door to remote access for a very large share of enterprises, sitting outside the perimeter, terminating sessions for staff and third parties, and holding the session material that makes lateral movement easy. Authentication-bypass bugs in this product line have repeatedly become an initial-access vector for ransomware affiliates within weeks of a proof of concept landing. Belgium’s national CSIRT has already told organisations to prioritise the patch. Note also what patching alone does not do — if a session was hijacked before you upgraded, the fix does not evict the attacker.

_threatfeed.source_name: BleepingComputer (Previdian telemetry); Citrix security bulletin; Shadowserver; NCC-BE
_threatfeed.date_note: Advisory 19 Aug 2026; exploitation observed 3 Sep 2026; reported 4 Sep 2026

items.title: An unpatched Magento and Adobe Commerce zero-day nicknamed StyleSmuggler is backdooring stores now — no CVE, no advisory and no vendor patch
items.content_text: Dutch e-commerce security firm Sansec published an advisory on 5 September reporting active exploitation of a previously unknown flaw in Magento Open Source and Adobe Commerce, which it named StyleSmuggler. Attacks were observed on 4 and 5 September. The described chain is two-stage: the attacker injects PHP into files that Magento itself generates, then triggers execution through the platform’s Payment Transaction Failed Reminder email function, giving unauthenticated remote code execution and a persistent backdoor. Sansec reports current releases affected, including Magento Open Source 2.4.7, 2.4.8 and 2.4.9, and says instances with the August 2026 updates applied were still compromised. As of this edition Adobe has not issued a CVE identifier, an advisory, a patch or an official workaround; its next scheduled security release is 8 September. That combination — confirmed exploitation, no vendor fix, no CVE to track against — is the worst state a widely deployed application can be in, and it is why this sits second on the radar despite affecting a narrower estate than the NetScaler bypass. Anyone whose organisation runs a storefront, including one owned by marketing or a subsidiary, is in scope. Treat unofficial community patches as risk-managed stopgaps, validated in a test environment, not as vendor-supported fixes.

_threatfeed.date_note: Exploitation observed 4–5 Sep 2026; advisory published 5 Sep 2026

items.title: CERT Polska says two MikroTik RouterOS SSH flaws are being chained for unauthenticated administrative takeover — attacks seen since 2 September
items.content_text: CERT Polska issued a warning on 5 September that MikroTik RouterOS vulnerabilities are being exploited in the wild. Two of them combine into what the team calls MikroTrick. CVE-2026-67276, CVSS 9.2, is an SSH authentication bypass caused by improper RSA public-key verification, allowing access without the private key. CVE-2026-86060, also CVSS 9.2, is an SSH privilege escalation reached through a crafted username beginning with a disallowed character, which yields full administrative privileges. Chained against a device with SSH reachable from the internet, the result is complete takeover with no credentials. A third issue, CVE-2026-67277 at CVSS 8.8, leaks kernel memory or restarts the device through the bandwidth-test service, and three further flaws affect the SSH client, X.509 certificate handling and the WebFig interface. MikroTik has published fixes in 7.25beta3, 7.24.2, 7.23.4 and 6.49.21. CERT Polska observed exploitation from at least 2 September, naming 82.192.72.4 as the primary source and 103.102.31.18 as making further attempts, and lists concrete log indicators: SSH login failures for a user named “-2”, creation of an account called “ops”, and unknown users or scripts appearing in the configuration. RouterOS turns up in enterprise networks more often than most inventories admit — branch offices, labs, temporary sites and equipment inherited through acquisition.

_threatfeed.date_note: Exploitation observed from 2 Sep 2026; CERT Polska warning 5 Sep 2026

items.title: JetBrains says attackers breached its Cadence cloud service through an unpatched TeamCity server and took AWS credentials, a full server backup and potentially customer source code
items.content_text: JetBrains disclosed that Cadence, the cloud compute service integrated with PyCharm, was compromised after attackers exploited CVE-2026-63077 — a critical TeamCity flaw allowing an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands on a vulnerable server. By JetBrains’ own account exploitation began on 8 August 2026, the breach was discovered on 23 August, the affected server was taken offline on 24 August, and the investigation concluded on 3 September. What the attackers obtained is unusually broad: usernames, real names, email addresses, login timestamps and IP addresses; a complete 2024 server backup containing credentials, configuration and artefacts; the AWS IAM credentials and secrets used by Cadence; files in JetBrains S3 buckets; and potentially source code synchronised from PyCharm projects. JetBrains is telling customers to treat every credential stored or used on the platform as compromised, to monitor connected systems including AWS, repositories and registries, to review source code for unauthorised changes, and to treat past project executions and their data as untrusted. Two things generalise. First, the entry point was an unpatched instance of the vendor’s own CI product — if a vendor can miss a TeamCity patch, so can you. Second, a developer cloud service holds the credentials of everyone who used it, so the blast radius of one server extends into every customer’s cloud account.

_threatfeed.source_name: JetBrains security incident disclosure; The Hacker News
_threatfeed.date_note: Exploitation from 8 Aug 2026; discovered 23 Aug; investigation concluded 3 Sep 2026

items.title: Coder’s module registry served credential-stealing Terraform modules for 14 hours after attackers added rogue servers to its Cloudflare pool
items.content_text: Coder, which provides self-hosted cloud development environments to organisations including large enterprises and government agencies, disclosed that attackers gained access to its Cloudflare infrastructure and added unauthorised IP addresses to the pool serving its module registry. For roughly fourteen hours on 31 August 2026, between 07:35 and 21:45 UTC, some requests were answered by attacker-controlled servers that returned trojanised Terraform modules. The modules functioned as information stealers, collecting API keys and cloud credentials, CI/CD pipeline secrets, SSH keys and authentication tokens, database passwords, and terminal history and configuration files, and exfiltrating them to the lookalike domain coder-infra[.]com. Coder has published fixed versions and guidance, but stated plainly that it has no access to the attacker’s infrastructure logs and therefore cannot conclusively identify every affected deployment. That is the detail worth carrying: absence of evidence here is genuinely not evidence of absence, and the correct default for any workspace that pulled modules in that window is to assume exposure. Note also the attack path — not the package registry itself but the DNS and edge layer in front of it, which is a control plane most organisations never think of as part of their software supply chain.

_threatfeed.date_note: Serving window 31 Aug 2026 07:35–21:45 UTC; reported 3 Sep 2026

items.title: Attackers are chaining two PaperCut NG/MF flaws to harvest credentials from schools and universities across the US and Europe
items.content_text: Arctic Wolf documented hands-on-keyboard activity following exploitation of two PaperCut NG/MF vulnerabilities that chain together with no authentication required: CVE-2026-81578, a missing-authentication flaw permitting configuration changes, and CVE-2026-82078, an unsafe-reflection issue allowing arbitrary Java bytecode execution. CISA added both to the KEV catalog on 31 August 2026. Once in, the operators behaved like any competent intrusion set rather than an automated scanner: reconnaissance commands such as uname, whoami, ver and tasklist; creation of privileged accounts including one named Administrator17; deployment of credential-harvesting tooling identified as lsa_collect.exe and save_hives.exe; extraction of registry hives to reach SAM databases; and Meterpreter Java payloads for persistence. Reported infrastructure includes 45.142.193[.]132 for malware delivery and 194.180.48[.]134 for Meterpreter command and control. Victims span K-12 schools through to major universities in the United States and Europe. The wider point for any sector: print management sits on a server almost nobody treats as sensitive, yet it is typically domain-joined, holds service accounts with broad rights, and integrates with directory and finance systems. It is a credential store wearing the badge of an office utility.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News (Arctic Wolf research); CISA KEV catalog
_threatfeed.date_note: KEV additions 31 Aug 2026; Arctic Wolf reporting 5 Sep 2026

items.title: The Shai-Hulud npm worm is still self-propagating and now scans 469 separate credential locations, up from 189
items.content_text: The self-replicating npm worm known as Shai-Hulud remains live and remains the broadest single exposure in the developer ecosystem. The current wave began at 09:00 UTC on 4 August 2026, when a compromised maintainer identity was used to publish malicious versions of widely used packages including keyv, cacheable-request, cache-manager, flat-cache and file-entry-cache. Wiz counted more than 400 distinct packages; Singapore’s CSA put the figure above 1,300 affected versions representing roughly two billion monthly downloads; JFrog later tracked the campaign across 1,700-plus versions. There is no CVE and no patch because nothing was flawed — packages were replaced. The payload runs from a preinstall hook under the Bun runtime, harvests npm tokens, GitHub PATs, cloud keys, Kubernetes secrets and AI service keys, then uses any writable publishing token to push infected releases of every package that identity can reach. It plants execution hooks in repository files such as .vscode/tasks.json and AI assistant hook configurations, and injects workflows to steal GitHub Actions secrets. Command-and-control addresses are read from an Ethereum smart contract, so domain takedowns achieve little. On 3 September GitGuardian reported the credential-scanning logic had grown from 189 paths to 469, now covering .env files, shell history, package-manager configs, CLI caches, CI/CD systems, IDE settings and AI tool configuration. The operators are not breaking trust relationships; they are collecting the credentials already lying around build environments.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News (GitGuardian research); JFrog Security Research; Wiz; CSA Singapore
_threatfeed.date_note: Campaign began 4 Aug 2026; expanded credential scope reported 3 Sep 2026

items.title: A dark-web service is selling 153 million driver’s licence scans, the FBI has opened an investigation, and identity-verification vendor IDScan is being sued
items.content_text: Security journalist Brian Krebs reported on 1 September that a dark-web identity-theft service calling itself Nexus was advertising access to 153 million US and Canadian driver’s licence scans, 10 million ID cards, 3 million travel documents and 579,000 medical cards; he verified the claim by locating his own record and those of consenting individuals. The FBI’s New Orleans office opened an investigation, later confirmed to BleepingComputer by both Reuters and the Bureau. Multiple lawsuits have been filed in Louisiana, where identity-verification vendor IDScan is based, alleging the company failed to protect data belonging to its clients. IDScan’s technology scans and extracts data from government-issued identity documents for car-rental firms, retailers, financial institutions, dispensaries and hospitality venues. Crucially, it is not established that IDScan’s own systems were breached or by what route the data was obtained; the company had not issued a public statement as of this edition, though it reportedly began notifying business customers around 1 September. The lesson for enterprise IT is not about this vendor. If your business asks customers or staff to present an ID at a counter, a kiosk or an onboarding flow, some processor is retaining an image of that document, and the retention period and blast radius of that store are almost never covered in the contract you signed.

_threatfeed.date_note: Initial reporting 1 Sep 2026; FBI confirmation and lawsuits reported 4–5 Sep 2026

items.title: More than 5,400 hacked websites are serving ClickFix lures whose payloads live on a public blockchain, making takedown effectively impossible
items.content_text: Netskope reported that over 5,400 compromised websites, mostly WordPress and PrestaShop installations, have been injected with scripts that fetch their payloads from the BNB Smart Chain testnet using the EtherHiding technique. Because the testnet is free to use and behaves like a production chain, the attackers get resilient, unremovable payload hosting with no infrastructure to seize. Visitors see a fake CAPTCHA that instructs them to open the Windows Run dialog and paste a PowerShell command — the ClickFix pattern — which pulls the malware down. Netskope tracked the campaign back to spring 2026, with roughly 400 infected sites contacting BNB Smart Chain endpoints daily by August and a peak of 536. The payload has since evolved from a straightforward downloader into a WebRTC data-channel stager that constructs its own answer rather than completing a normal handshake, establishing a covert encrypted channel for remote code execution that does not look like web traffic. Two defensive implications follow. First, ClickFix defeats every control that assumes the user has to be tricked into opening a file — the user is the execution engine, so the countermeasures are user education and restricting the Run dialog and PowerShell for standard users. Second, the payload channel is neither HTTP nor DNS, so egress monitoring that only watches those two will not see the second stage.

_threatfeed.date_note: Campaign from spring 2026; reported 5 Sep 2026

items.title: Manchester Airports Group data on roughly 8.8 million people was leaked after the group refused to pay — the reported entry point was an API key sitting in public page JavaScript
items.content_text: Manchester Airports Group, operator of Manchester, London Stansted and East Midlands airports, detected unauthorised access on 25 August 2026 and disclosed the breach on 27 August. Around 8.8 million people were affected, with data drawn from car-park bookings, lounge and Fast Track purchases and airport Wi-Fi registrations. Payment card data was not involved and flight operations were unaffected. MAG refused the extortion demand, and by 3 September the data had been published. The extortion group FulcrumSec claimed responsibility and, per SecurityWeek, published roughly 550 GB — names, emails, phone numbers, town and postal region, residential IP addresses, vehicle registration plates, parking and lounge booking details and associated SMS messages. Their account of the method is what every IT team should sit with: they say they found an API key for Iterable, MAG’s marketing-automation platform, embedded in publicly readable page JavaScript, and then simply called the API. MAG has not confirmed the specifics, so treat the mechanism as claimed rather than established. But a client-side secret is a failure mode that requires no vulnerability, leaves no exploit signature and is invisible to every vulnerability scanner you own. The residual risk to individuals is high-quality phishing: knowing someone’s travel dates, terminal and car registration makes a convincing lure.

_threatfeed.source_name: SecurityWeek; IT Security Guru; BleepingComputer contact with FulcrumSec
_threatfeed.date_note: Detected 25 Aug 2026; disclosed 27 Aug; data leaked and reported 3 Sep 2026

items.title: Datadog tracked a month-long password-spraying campaign against AWS root user accounts at more than 150 organisations
items.content_text: Datadog Security Research published findings on 31 August describing a campaign that ran from 24 July to 23 August 2026 and attempted to authenticate as the AWS root user across more than 150 organisations, with no clear industry or geographic focus. The technique was deliberately quiet: a small set of common or previously exposed passwords tried against many accounts, which keeps each account below lockout thresholds. The median organisation saw two failed attempts; some saw as many as eight. Requests came from geographically dispersed IP addresses across multiple autonomous systems using proxy, residential-proxy or hosting infrastructure, with spoofed user agents impersonating Microsoft Edge on Chrome 85 and Firefox 120. Datadog identified no successful authentications. That is the useful part of this report rather than a disappointment: it shows attackers systematically working through root email addresses they have harvested or guessed, and it means the detection is available to you before the compromise rather than after. Root is the one identity in an AWS account that cannot be constrained by IAM policy, so a single success is a total loss of that account.

_threatfeed.date_note: Campaign 24 Jul – 23 Aug 2026; published 31 Aug 2026

items.title: FortiGuard Labs documents LLMjacking: a leaked AWS IAM key turned into six-figure daily inference bills through Amazon Bedrock
items.content_text: FortiGuard Labs described a now well-established monetisation path for stolen cloud credentials. An attacker obtains a long-lived IAM access key carrying administrator rights, creates a new IAM user inside the victim’s account, then issues CreateAgreementRequest and AcceptAgreementRequest calls to subscribe the account to foundation models through AWS Marketplace and invokes them directly, with the inference charges billed to the victim. A secondary technique generates Bedrock service-specific API keys so the subsequent calls look less conspicuous. The reported economics are striking: abuse of Claude 2.x generating more than $46,000 a day, and Claude 3 Opus more than $100,000 a day. One tracked campaign, referred to as Operation Bizarre Bazaar, is linked to over 35,000 attack sessions across more than 30 LLM providers, with the stolen access resold as discounted AI subscriptions through Telegram and Discord. What makes this hard to catch is that every API call is technically valid and properly permissioned, so it looks like a team suddenly adopting AI. Note that Bedrock invocation logging is off by default — if you have not turned it on, the first signal you get is the invoice.

_threatfeed.date_note: Reported 4 Sep 2026

items.title: Elastic finds four REVSTEALER modules that disable Windows Update and Defender to run a miner — and the damage outlives the malware
items.content_text: Elastic Security Labs published research on 2 September documenting four post-infection modules linked to REVSTEALER, an information stealer sold commercially since at least February 2026. ProManager steals wallet files and browser wallet extensions and overlays attacker-controlled content on a wallet application’s window. WinUpdate watches the clipboard and swaps cryptocurrency addresses. SoftManager turns the machine into a reverse proxy that routes attacker traffic through the victim’s connection. LockAppHost runs a cryptocurrency miner after suppressing defences: it abuses the Windows CMSTP tool to obtain administrator rights, disables five Windows Update services and eleven scheduled update tasks, adds Microsoft Defender exclusions for common folders and file types, and removes two malware-removal tasks. Delivery is largely through game-cheat lures on hijacked YouTube channels with AI-generated videos, plus fake software installers — including one impersonating an AI desktop application. The miner runs with administrator rights inside suspended instances of legitimate processes such as nslookup.exe or svchost.exe. The part that matters for enterprise IT is the persistence of the sabotage: those disabled services, tasks and Defender exclusions remain after the malware is removed, so a machine that was cleaned and returned to the user may have been silently unpatched and unprotected ever since.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News (Elastic Security Labs research)
_threatfeed.date_note: Elastic report 2 Sep 2026; coverage 6 Sep 2026

items.title: Rapid7 finds the Ted backdoor compiled directly into victims’ own HAProxy load balancers, hiding command traffic inside ordinary web responses
items.content_text: Rapid7 Labs documented a previously undocumented Linux toolkit that the operators appear to call “ted”, based on debug strings in the binary. Rather than installing an implant alongside the load balancer, the attackers recompiled HAProxy itself with the backdoor built in, then deployed it in place of the legitimate binary. Requests for specific image paths put the load balancer into command mode; commands are written to a named pipe under /tmp, and responses return over a raw socket with ordinary HTTP/1.0 200 OK headers. The implant decrements connection counters so its own sessions do not appear in statistics, rewrites content type, length and status, and strips Accept-Ranges headers so clients cannot detect size changes. Two South Korean organisations, in the automotive and media sectors, were found running HAProxy 2.8.12. Rapid7 hypothesises initial access through an exposed Korean enterprise groupware portal and attributes the toolkit to North Korean state-sponsored activity with medium confidence, citing overlap with APT37, Lazarus and Kimsuky clusters. The generalisable warning is uncomfortable: a recompiled HAProxy reports the same version string as a legitimate build, so version-based inventory and vulnerability scanning will tell you the device is fine.

_threatfeed.date_note: Reported 4 Sep 2026

items.title: Recorded Future ties the HOOKEDGE backdoor to APT28, using webhook.site for command and control and hidden Edge windows to exfiltrate
items.content_text: Recorded Future’s Insikt Group documented HOOKEDGE, a lightweight Windows batch-script backdoor used against government and diplomatic organisations in Romania, Spain and Türkiye between late September 2025 and early April 2026. Initial access came through macro-enabled Microsoft Word documents with diplomatic lures; enabling content writes six files to the user profile directory and starts the chain. The backdoor polls webhook staging endpoints, retrieves .cmd payloads, executes them and returns results through hidden Microsoft Edge instances. Command and control, payload staging and exfiltration all run through webhook.site, which lets the activity blend into ordinary web traffic; a two-stage architecture separates initial access from active collection infrastructure to work around that service’s hundred-request-per-endpoint limit. Recorded Future attributes the toolkit to APT28 — also tracked as Fancy Bear, Forest Blizzard and, in their naming, BlueDelta — with moderate confidence, based on code and tradecraft overlap with the HEADLACE backdoor. The technique is what travels beyond the diplomatic target set: legitimate webhook and automation services are broadly allow-listed, rarely inspected, and give an operator a fully hosted C2 channel with no infrastructure to attribute or seize.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News (Recorded Future Insikt Group research)
_threatfeed.date_note: Campaign late Sep 2025 – early Apr 2026; reported 27–28 Aug 2026

items.title: Google patched the sixth Chrome zero-day of 2026 — CVE-2026-85046, a V8 type confusion already exploited in the wild, added to KEV the same day
items.content_text: Google released a Chrome update on 4 September 2026 fixing CVE-2026-85046, a type-confusion flaw in V8, the browser’s JavaScript and WebAssembly engine, and stated that an exploit for it exists in the wild. The fixed builds are 152.0.7977.82 and .83 on Windows and macOS and 152.0.7977.82 on Linux. The bug allows a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code inside the renderer sandbox through a crafted HTML page; the underlying defect gives arrays incorrect memory maps, yielding arbitrary read and write access to the JavaScript heap. It was reported on 4 August 2026 by researcher Salvatore Gulizia. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 4 September. This is the sixth Chrome zero-day patched in 2026, following CVE-2026-2441, CVE-2026-3909, CVE-2026-3910, CVE-2026-5281 and CVE-2026-11645. Two practical notes. Chrome updates on restart, so a fleet where people never close the browser is a fleet that is not patched — check your actual version distribution rather than assuming auto-update worked. And every Chromium-based browser in your estate inherits this: Edge, Brave, Opera, Vivaldi and any embedded Electron application need their own updates on their own vendor schedules.

_threatfeed.source_name: Help Net Security; SecurityWeek; CISA KEV catalog
_threatfeed.date_note: Reported to Google 4 Aug 2026; patched and KEV-listed 4 Sep 2026

items.title: SonicWall discloses two SMA1000 zero-days it has already seen chained in attacks — a CVSS 10.0 pre-auth SSRF plus command injection
items.content_text: SonicWall disclosed on 2 September 2026 that it found two vulnerabilities in the SMA1000 series internally and has observed exploitation of both, which suggests they are being chained. CVE-2026-83548, rated CVSS 10.0, is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface that lets an unauthenticated remote attacker reach sensitive functionality and perform unauthorised operations. CVE-2026-83549, CVSS 7.8, is an OS command injection in the Appliance Management Console that lets an authenticated attacker run arbitrary operating-system commands, leading to remote code execution. Affected models are the SMA1000 series 6210, 7210 and 8200v; fixes are in hotfixes 12.4.3-03526 and 12.5.0-02952 and later. SonicWall SSL-VPN on firewalls and the SMA100 series are not affected. CISA added CVE-2026-83548 and CVE-2026-83549 to the KEV catalog on 2 September. No public indicators of compromise have been released, which makes detection harder than usual — this is one where you cannot wait for an IOC list before acting. The SMA1000 line has now been through repeated exploited zero-days, and for organisations still running it the strategic question is whether the product remains the right choice for internet-facing remote access.

_threatfeed.date_note: Disclosed and KEV-listed 2 Sep 2026

items.title: Sangoma Switchvox is under active exploitation — one crafted request gives unauthenticated SQL injection and remote code execution on an enterprise phone system
items.content_text: CVE-2026-9586, rated CVSS 9.3, is an unauthenticated SQL injection in Sangoma Switchvox, an enterprise VoIP telephony management platform. The flaw sits in an XML-processing endpoint that concatenates a user-controlled PhoneIP value into PostgreSQL queries without sanitising it. Per NIST, an unauthenticated remote attacker can execute arbitrary SQL against the backend database with a single crafted request, including operations that lead to remote code execution. Horizon3 confirmed in-the-wild exploitation on 3 September 2026 and published indicators of compromise. CISA listed the flaw in its KEV catalog in the seven-CVE batch of 2 September, and under BOD 26-04 federal agencies face a three-day remediation window rather than the usual longer clock — a useful signal of how CISA is reading the urgency. Telephony platforms are a familiar blind spot: they are frequently managed by facilities or a telecoms provider rather than by IT security, they often sit on a flat voice VLAN with routes into the corporate network, and they hold call records and directory data that are useful for social engineering. If you do not know who patches your phone system, that is the finding.

_threatfeed.source_name: SecurityWeek (Horizon3 research, NIST record); CISA KEV catalog
_threatfeed.date_note: Exploitation confirmed 3 Sep 2026; reported 4 Sep 2026

items.title: HPE patches an unauthenticated remote-code-execution flaw in ArubaOS-CX switches, CVSS 9.8, alongside 23 further high-severity issues
items.content_text: HPE published a bulletin fixing CVE-2026-73749, a buffer overflow in an ArubaOS-CX daemon that allows unauthenticated remote code execution with elevated privileges when specially crafted packets are sent to the affected service. Fixed builds are 10.18.1002 and later for 10.18.0001; 10.17.1030 and later for 10.17.1021 and earlier; 10.16.1060 and later for 10.16.1051 and earlier; 10.13.1190 and later for 10.13.1180 and earlier; and 10.10.1181 and later for 10.10.1180 and earlier. Twenty-three further vulnerabilities carrying CVSS scores from 8.1 to 8.8 were fixed in the same bulletin, including CVE-2026-73750 (denial of service or code execution via malformed input, authenticated), CVE-2026-73751 (arbitrary command execution through the web interface, authenticated), CVE-2026-73752 (arbitrary file writes via an API endpoint, adjacent network), CVE-2026-73779 (authentication bypass, adjacent network) and CVE-2026-73778 (exploitation of a factory-default password). At bulletin publication HPE knew of no active exploitation and no public proof-of-concept exploit. That is the window to act in. Core and distribution switches are the hardest devices in the estate to schedule downtime for, which is precisely why they end up years behind — and a switch that executes attacker code has no meaningful containment story.

_threatfeed.date_note: Bulletin and reporting 3 Sep 2026

items.title: Wordfence has blocked more than 440,000 exploit attempts against Super Forms and Elementor Pro, and Elementor Pro site takeovers are now confirmed
items.content_text: Two unauthenticated file-upload flaws in widely installed WordPress plugins remain under sustained attack. CVE-2026-14894 in Super Forms, rated CVSS 9.8, is a missing file-type validation issue: attackers post Base64-encoded PHP to /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php through the super_submit_form endpoint and drop a web shell. Exploitation began on 14 July 2026 and peaked on 18 August at more than 40,000 requests a day, with over 250,000 attempts blocked in total; the fix is Super Forms 6.3.314. CVE-2026-32475 in Elementor Pro, disclosed through Patchstack in August and fixed in 4.2.2, is a validation bypass reached by submitting a form’s File Upload field as an array, landing PHP files under /wp-content/uploads/elementor/forms/. Attacks on that one started 19 August and account for a further 190,000-plus blocked attempts, and both BleepingComputer and SecurityWeek reported on 3–5 September that the Elementor Pro flaw is being used to take over sites. The combined total passed 440,000. This matters beyond marketing sites: WordPress instances are frequently run by a business unit rather than central IT, on infrastructure that still sits inside the corporate network or shares an identity provider, and a PHP web shell on such a host is a foothold like any other. Both campaigns are opportunistic and internet-wide, so exposure is a function of patch latency alone.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News (Wordfence telemetry, Patchstack advisory); SecurityWeek
_threatfeed.date_note: Super Forms attacks from 14 Jul 2026; Elementor Pro attacks from 19 Aug 2026; reported 4–5 Sep 2026

items.title: Roughly 3.2 million WordPress sites are still running a vulnerable All-in-One WP Migration build three weeks after the fix shipped
items.content_text: Defiant disclosed CVE-2026-19949, a second-order SQL injection in the archive-restore functionality of All-in-One WP Migration and Backup, a plugin with more than five million active installations. Rated CVSS 8.8, the flaw lets an unauthenticated attacker extract the secret key used during archive restoration and then install a malicious plugin, giving remote code execution and full site compromise. The mechanism is worth understanding because it is unusual: the attacker submits trackbacks containing trailing backslashes and a malicious payload URL, and when an administrator later performs a restore, the plugin rewrites the SQL in a way that promotes the attacker’s input to executable SQL, writing the secret key into a publicly visible comment. In other words, the attacker plants the trap and waits for a routine administrative action to spring it. Version 7.110 fixed the issue on 20 August 2026, but as of 3 September only around 35% of installations had updated, leaving approximately 3.2 million sites on a vulnerable build. Active exploitation had not been confirmed at the time of reporting — which, given the install base and the simplicity of the trigger, is best read as a head start rather than a reprieve.

_threatfeed.date_note: Fix released 20 Aug 2026; reported 3 Sep 2026

items.title: CISA added eight vulnerabilities to the KEV catalog in five days, and half of them sit in developer and AI infrastructure
items.content_text: Between 31 August and 4 September 2026 CISA made three additions to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. On 31 August it listed the two PaperCut NG/MF flaws, CVE-2026-81578 and CVE-2026-82078. On 2 September it added seven entries: CVE-2026-83548 and CVE-2026-83549 in SonicWall SMA1000; CVE-2026-82329, an improper-authentication flaw in JFrog Artifactory allowing unauthenticated administrative access; CVE-2026-49869, an OS command injection in the Kestra orchestration platform permitting unauthenticated workflow execution; CVE-2026-48710, HTTP request and response smuggling in the Starlette Python framework; CVE-2026-59822, an improper-authentication flaw in BerriAI LiteLLM; and CVE-2026-9586, the Sangoma Switchvox SQL injection. On 4 September it added CVE-2026-85046, the Chrome V8 zero-day. The composition is the story. Artifactory, Kestra, Starlette and LiteLLM are all developer or AI plumbing — artefact registries, workflow orchestration, a web framework and an LLM gateway. Reporting on the 2 September batch described attackers using them to open reverse shells, mint administrative tokens and drop XMRig miners. These systems typically sit inside the perimeter with generous cloud roles, weak authentication and no endpoint coverage, which is what turns a web-layer bug into cloud role takeover in one step.

_threatfeed.source_name: CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog; The Hacker News
_threatfeed.date_note: KEV additions 31 Aug, 2 Sep and 4 Sep 2026

items.title: Broadcom patches a CVSS 9.3 VMware Workstation and Fusion flaw that lets an admin inside a VM execute code on the host
items.content_text: Broadcom published fixes for two VMware Workstation and Fusion vulnerabilities. CVE-2026-59346, rated CVSS 9.3, is an integer overflow reachable by an attacker with local administrative privileges on a virtual machine configured with a VMXNET3 network adapter, and it allows arbitrary code execution on the host. CVE-2026-59347, CVSS 8.1, is a stack-based buffer overflow that similarly requires local administrative privileges inside a guest and permits code execution as the VMX process on the host. Both affect Workstation and Fusion 25H2 and 26H1 and are fixed in 26H1u1. Both were disclosed privately, and neither has known in-the-wild exploitation. There are no workarounds, so patching is the only route. The reason this belongs on an enterprise page rather than a hobbyist one is the malware-analysis and development use case: security teams, developers and support staff run untrusted code inside desktop hypervisors precisely because they believe the guest boundary holds. A guest-to-host escape inverts that assumption on the machines belonging to the people with the most access. SecurityWeek notes that more than 25 VMware issues already appear in CISA’s KEV catalog, which is a fair guide to how much attention this product family attracts.

_threatfeed.date_note: Reported 4 Sep 2026

items.title: A public proof of concept named FalconFlank escalates to SYSTEM through CrowdStrike Falcon’s own macro-remediation feature
items.content_text: A researcher operating as Chaotic Eclipse published a proof of concept on GitHub on 3 September 2026 demonstrating local privilege escalation by abusing the CrowdStrike Falcon sensor’s Office malicious-macro remediation function. The researcher reports it working on fully updated Windows 11 25H2 and Windows Server 2025. No CVE has been assigned, and there is no evidence of in-the-wild exploitation. CrowdStrike says it is actively investigating the claims and has advised customers to disable the Microsoft Office File Suspicious Macro Removal Windows policy setting while continuing to rely on the Cloud Anti-malware for Microsoft Office Files settings. This is a local escalation, not remote code execution, so it needs an attacker who is already on the host — which is why it sits at Medium here rather than higher. But the class of issue deserves attention out of proportion to its severity rating: endpoint agents run with the highest privilege available, are installed on effectively every machine, and are exempted from the controls that constrain other software. A privilege-escalation primitive inside the security agent is a reliable second step for any commodity infection, and it is not one your EDR will flag.

_threatfeed.date_note: PoC published 3 Sep 2026; reported 4 Sep 2026

items.title: The stopgap funding bill extends the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 into early December — the fourth short-term rescue of a law nobody wants to renew permanently
items.content_text: A continuing resolution passed by the House and previously approved by the Senate extends the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 through the stopgap funding period into early December 2026. The law is what gives companies liability protection when they share cyber threat indicators with government agencies and with each other, and without it many corporate legal departments will not approve participation in information-sharing arrangements at all. Its recent history is a study in how fragile that foundation is: it briefly lapsed during last autumn’s shutdown, lapsed again earlier before being extended to 30 September, and is now carried again on the back of a funding bill rather than reauthorised on its own terms. Industry associations continue to press for a permanent solution, while Senator Rand Paul has blocked bipartisan reauthorisation efforts pending free-speech provisions he wants included. Federal News Network notes that the Treasury Department’s new GOLD EAGLE cybersecurity clearinghouse depends on these protections. For an enterprise, the practical exposure is that the legal basis for your ISAC participation and your threat-intelligence sharing agreements has a three-month expiry date attached to a budget negotiation.

_threatfeed.date_note: Reported 3 Sep 2026; extension runs into early December 2026

items.title: France’s CNIL fines a private hospital €500,000 — and half the penalty is about who was never told, not how the attacker got in
items.content_text: On 3 September 2026 the CNIL fined Hôpital Privé de la Loire €500,000 following a breach in which an attacker accessed the hospital’s computerised patient record system in summer 2025, exposing data on 524,867 patients and 202,246 designated trusted third parties. The regulator found violations of GDPR Article 32 on security and Article 34 on communicating a breach to data subjects. The security failings named are notable for how ordinary they are: authentication without VPN or multi-factor protection, access controls that let a single user’s credentials reach every patient record, no real-time monitoring for suspicious activity, and consequently no detection of an extraction that ran over several days. The Article 34 finding is the one worth carrying into your own planning — the hospital notified affected patients but did not notify the 202,246 trusted third parties whose data was also involved, which the CNIL held deprived those individuals of information they needed to understand the incident. Breach notification is routinely scoped to the obvious population of data subjects, and secondary populations such as emergency contacts, guarantors, referees, next of kin and beneficiaries are exactly the ones a hurried notification exercise leaves out.

_threatfeed.date_note: Breach summer 2025; CNIL decision 3 Sep 2026

items.title: CISA still expects to finalise the CIRCIA incident-reporting rule this month — 72 hours for incidents, 24 hours for ransom payments
items.content_text: CISA has targeted September 2026 for publication of the final rule implementing the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act of 2022. As proposed, covered entities in critical-infrastructure sectors would have to report substantial cyber incidents to CISA within 72 hours and any ransom payment within 24 hours. The rule has slipped repeatedly: the statutory deadline was October 2025, CISA’s own prior internal target was May 2026, and the agency held town-hall consultations in June 2026 with more than 1,200 participants before settling on the current timeline. Final thresholds for who counts as a covered entity — based on the sector and size criteria set out in the April 2024 proposed rule — remain pending, which is precisely the detail most organisations need in order to know whether they are in scope. Carried here as still-current rather than new: the September target was set in July and had not been superseded as of this edition. The reason to prepare regardless of the publication date is that a 72-hour clock is short if nobody has decided in advance who declares an incident reportable, who writes the report and who signs it. Organisations already reporting under NIS2, DORA, SEC disclosure rules or state regulations should be mapping CIRCIA against those obligations now rather than building a separate process.

_threatfeed.source_name: Hunton Andrews Kurth privacy and cybersecurity blog (CISA regulatory agenda)
_threatfeed.date_note: Reported 17 Jul 2026; final rule targeted for September 2026
